headline: High-risk write-capability overlap and default data-flow from ComfyUI into OpenHands can cause cascading errors and compliance-sensitive leakage.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ComfyUI has no stdin/stdout, clipboard, or MCP bridge, so direct injection is not default. OpenHands can use MCP and browser/shell tools, but the pair lacks a documented shared channel. Any prompt-injection path would require unusual manual bridging or file handoff, so blast radius is small.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies ComfyUI outputs into OpenHands prompts or files, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared MCP server or shared workspace is added, the pathway strengthens.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Disable manual copy-paste of generated text into OpenHands.
Do not connect both agents to the same MCP server.
Use a review step before any OpenHands prompt includes ComfyUI output.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ComfyUI touches images, videos, audio, models, and checkpoints, while OpenHands reads and writes files in its runtime and can use mounted volumes. If the same workspace or mounted volume is shared, OpenHands can ingest ComfyUI artifacts and potentially transmit them via its broad network egress. The pair therefore has a default-available leakage path once co-located.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted volume or directory tree, leakage becomes plausible.
IF OpenHands is configured to send runtime files to a model provider, artifacts can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate directories for ComfyUI and OpenHands.
Mount ComfyUI outputs read-only into OpenHands.
Remove sensitive images and checkpoints before sharing files.
Restrict OpenHands network egress where possible.
Audit which files OpenHands loads before each run.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ComfyUI can write model files and operates with an asynchronous queue, while OpenHands has shell, filesystem write, git modification, and root-in-Docker privileges. If they share a mounted volume, both can mutate the same files without documented locking, creating a real default conflict risk and possible irreversible corruption of workflows or models.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same mounted directory, file clobbering is possible.
IF OpenHands edits git-tracked assets that ComfyUI also reads, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint write directories.
Make shared model assets read-only.
Avoid letting OpenHands modify ComfyUI-managed files.
Use snapshots before concurrent runs.
Pause one agent while the other writes shared assets.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can act on files and shell commands, so if it treats ComfyUI-generated outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes, commits, or runtime actions. ComfyUI produces generated artifacts rather than verified facts, and no verification bridge is documented between the pair, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses ComfyUI output as a source of truth without human review, cascading error risk is present.
IF OpenHands commits or executes actions derived from generated content, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Require human review of ComfyUI outputs before OpenHands acts.
Label generated content as untrusted in the workflow.
Block automatic commit or execution steps from generated artifacts.
Add a verification checklist for any downstream action.
Keep generation and action-taking in separate sessions.

E_compliance.rationale: ComfyUI processes media and model assets locally, while OpenHands handles files in a runtime sandbox and may send context to a configured model provider. If regulated images or secrets are placed into the shared runtime, OpenHands can move them to a third-party backend, creating a compliance mismatch. The pair is open-source, but the runtime/network behavior makes the risk nontrivial.
conditions: IF regulated data is loaded into OpenHands's runtime, provider-bound transmission may violate policy.
IF the deployment requires strict residency or retention controls, shared handling can breach them.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of OpenHands runs.
Use a local-only model provider for sensitive tasks.
Delete sensitive runtime files immediately after use.
Document retention and residency expectations for both tools.
Separate compliant and noncompliant workloads.
